questions.stem: Acetazolamide lowers intraocular pressure in glaucoma primarily through which mechanism?
options: Contracting the ciliary muscle to open the trabecular meshwork
Increasing uveoscleral outflow of aqueous humor
Blocking sympathetic beta receptors on the ciliary body
Decreasing aqueous humor production by the ciliary epithelium
explanations: Incorrect - contraction of the ciliary muscle to open the trabecular meshwork describes the mechanism of parasympathomimetics like pilocarpine, not acetazolamide.
Incorrect - increased uveoscleral outflow describes the mechanism of prostaglandin analogues, not acetazolamide.
Incorrect - blocking beta receptors describes the mechanism of beta blockers (e.g., timolol), not acetazolamide, which works via carbonic anhydrase inhibition.

Correct - acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, decreases aqueous humor production by the ciliary epithelium, acting as a diuretic to reduce intraocular pressure; it is also used in acute angle-closure glaucoma.
questions.overview: Acetazolamide is an oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that decreases aqueous humor production by the ciliary epithelium, used in both chronic glaucoma management and as emergency treatment for acute angle-closure glaucoma alongside mannitol.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with a 20-year history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes undergoes a routine dilated eye exam. Fundoscopy reveals abnormal, friable new blood vessels growing on the surface of the retina. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism driving this finding?
options: Embolic occlusion of the central retinal artery
Accumulation of drusen between Bruch's membrane and the retinal pigment epithelium
Autoimmune demyelination of the optic nerve
Increased intraocular pressure damaging the optic disc
Retinal ischemia leading to increased vascular endothelial growth factor
explanations: Incorrect - central retinal artery occlusion causes acute painless vision loss with a cherry-red spot, not neovascularization.
Incorrect - drusen accumulation is the hallmark of dry age-related macular degeneration, not proliferative diabetic retinopathy.
Incorrect - demyelination of the optic nerve describes optic neuritis, unrelated to retinal neovascularization.
Incorrect - elevated intraocular pressure causing optic disc cupping describes glaucoma, not proliferative diabetic retinopathy.

Correct - proliferative diabetic retinopathy results from retinal ischemia (from microvascular damage) that stimulates VEGF-driven neovascularization, producing friable new vessels on the retinal surface that can cause vitreous hemorrhage and retinal detachment.
questions.overview: Proliferative diabetic retinopathy develops when chronic retinal ischemia (from pericyte loss and microaneurysms) drives VEGF-mediated neovascularization; these new vessels are fragile and can bleed into the vitreous or cause tractional retinal detachment. Treatment includes laser photocoagulation, anti-VEGF injections, and vitrectomy, making regular screening essential in diabetics.

questions.stem: The sympathetic pathway controlling pupillary dilation is a three-neuron chain. At which location does the first-order neuron synapse to become the second-order neuron?
explanations: Incorrect - the ciliary ganglion is part of the parasympathetic pathway for pupillary constriction via CN III, unrelated to the sympathetic dilation pathway.
Correct - the first-order sympathetic neuron descends from the hypothalamus and synapses at the ciliospinal center of Budge (C8-T2) in the spinal cord, becoming the second-order neuron.
Incorrect - the superior cervical ganglion is the site where the second-order neuron synapses onto the third-order neuron, not the first synapse.
Incorrect - the cavernous sinus is where the third-order neuron travels alongside the internal carotid artery, not a synaptic site.
questions.overview: Pupillary dilation (mydriasis) is mediated by a three-neuron sympathetic chain: from the hypothalamus to the ciliospinal center of Budge (C8-T2), then to the superior cervical ganglion (exiting at T1, crossing the lung apex), then along the internal carotid artery through the cavernous sinus to the dilator pupillae. Disruption anywhere along this pathway causes Horner syndrome.

questions.stem: A patient presents with progressive loss of peripheral vision in both temporal visual fields. Imaging reveals a pituitary macroadenoma. Which anatomic structure is being compressed to produce this visual field defect?
options: Meyer's loop in the temporal lobe
explanations: Incorrect - lateral geniculate nucleus lesions also cause homonymous visual field defects, not bitemporal hemianopsia.
Incorrect - Meyer's loop lesions in the temporal lobe cause a contralateral superior quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky'), not bitemporal hemianopsia.
Incorrect - a lesion of the optic tract (beyond the chiasm) causes homonymous hemianopsia (loss of the same visual field in both eyes), not bitemporal loss.

Correct - the optic chiasm, located at the base of the brain beneath the hypothalamus and above the pituitary gland, contains crossing fibers from the medial (nasal) retina of both eyes; compression here (e.g., by a pituitary tumor) causes bitemporal hemianopsia.
questions.overview: The optic chiasm carries crossing fibers from the nasal (medial) retina of both eyes, which correspond to the temporal visual fields; compression at the chiasm, classically by a pituitary tumor, craniopharyngioma, or anterior communicating artery aneurysm, produces bitemporal hemianopsia.
questions.topic: Optic chiasm compression by pituitary adenoma

questions.stem: Which of the following distinguishes wet age-related macular degeneration from dry age-related macular degeneration?
options: Higher overall prevalence among AMD cases
Neovascularization due to increased VEGF with a break in Bruch's membrane
Slow, gradual progression of central vision loss
Accumulation of drusen between Bruch's membrane and the retinal pigment epithelium
explanations: Incorrect - dry AMD is more common (about 80% of cases) compared to wet AMD (10-15%).

Correct - wet AMD is characterized by a break in Bruch's membrane with retinal neovascularization driven by increased VEGF, leading to potential hemorrhage and rapid vision changes; it is treated with anti-VEGF agents and laser therapy.
Incorrect - slow, gradual progression is typical of dry AMD; wet AMD tends to progress rapidly (days to weeks).
Incorrect - drusen accumulation is characteristic of dry AMD, not wet AMD.
questions.overview: Age-related macular degeneration has two forms: dry AMD (more common, ~80%), characterized by drusen accumulation and slowly progressive RPE atrophy, and wet AMD (~10-15%), characterized by VEGF-driven neovascularization through a break in Bruch's membrane, causing rapid vision changes treated with anti-VEGF therapy.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history presents with a 3-week history of a drooping right eyelid. Examination shows right-sided ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis of the right face. Chest CT reveals a mass at the right lung apex invading the brachial plexus. Which of the following best explains the pupillary finding in this patient?
options: Interruption of the sympathetic chain supplying the dilator pupillae
Interruption of parasympathetic fibers traveling with CN III
Blockade of muscarinic receptors on the sphincter pupillae
Compression of the optic nerve by the apical mass
explanations: Incorrect - the Edinger-Westphal nucleus is part of the parasympathetic pupillary constriction pathway via CN III; a lesion here would impair miosis via CN III, not cause Horner syndrome.

Correct - a Pancoast tumor disrupts the three-neuron sympathetic chain (from the hypothalamus, through the ciliospinal center of Budge at C8-T2, across the lung apex to the superior cervical ganglion), causing loss of dilator pupillae activation (miosis), ptosis (loss of superior tarsal muscle innervation), and anhidrosis.
Incorrect - a CN III parasympathetic lesion causes mydriasis (dilated pupil), not miosis; this presentation is a Pancoast tumor causing Horner syndrome via sympathetic disruption.
Incorrect - muscarinic blockade would cause mydriasis, not miosis.
Incorrect - optic nerve compression would cause vision loss or an afferent pupillary defect, not the classic Horner triad.
questions.overview: Horner syndrome results from disruption of the three-neuron oculosympathetic pathway to the face and eye, producing ptosis (loss of superior tarsal muscle), miosis (unopposed parasympathetic constriction), and anhidrosis. Common causes include apical lung (Pancoast) tumors, carotid/aortic dissection, and lateral medullary (PICA) stroke. Cocaine drops fail to dilate the affected pupil, while apraclonidine paradoxically dilates it due to denervation supersensitivity.

questions.stem: A patient with a trochlear nerve (CN IV) palsy would be expected to have the most difficulty with which of the following activities?
options: Looking laterally away from the nose
Reading a book or walking down stairs
Constricting the pupil in bright light
explanations: Incorrect - eyelid elevation is performed by the levator palpebrae, innervated by the oculomotor nerve (CN III), not CN IV.
Incorrect - lateral gaze is controlled by the abducens nerve (CN VI) via the lateral rectus, not the trochlear nerve.

Correct - the trochlear nerve innervates the superior oblique muscle, which turns the eye down and intorts it; patients with CN IV palsy have difficulty with downward gaze, causing problems with activities like reading or walking down stairs, and often tilt their head away from the affected side to compensate.
Incorrect - pupillary constriction is mediated by parasympathetic fibers traveling with CN III, not CN IV.
questions.overview: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) innervates the superior oblique muscle, which turns the eye downward and inward (intorsion). CN IV palsy causes vertical diplopia and difficulty with downward gaze (e.g., reading, stairs), often compensated by tilting the head away from the affected side.

questions.stem: A patient started on latanoprost eye drops for glaucoma should be counseled about which of the following potential side effects?
options: Foreign body sensation with ocular hyperemia
explanations: Incorrect - blurry vision in low light is a side effect of parasympathomimetics (e.g., pilocarpine), not prostaglandin analogues.
Incorrect - foreign body sensation and ocular hyperemia are associated with alpha agonists (e.g., brimonidine), not prostaglandin analogues.
Incorrect - bradycardia and bronchospasm are side effects of beta blockers (e.g., timolol) used for glaucoma, not prostaglandin analogues.
Correct - prostaglandin analogues like latanoprost increase aqueous humor outflow via the uveoscleral pathway and are known to cause darkening of the iris as a side effect.
questions.overview: Prostaglandin analogues (bimatoprost, latanoprost, tafluprost, travoprost) treat glaucoma by increasing aqueous humor outflow through the uveoscleral pathway; a distinctive side effect is darkening/pigmentation of the iris, unlike other glaucoma drug classes.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child is found to have decreased visual acuity in one eye due to abnormal visual development during early childhood, related to a history of untreated strabismus. Which of the following terms best describes this condition?
explanations: Incorrect - astigmatism is a refractive error from uneven corneal curvature causing multiple focal points, not a cortical developmental problem.
Incorrect - presbyopia is age-related stiffening of the lens causing difficulty focusing on near objects, unrelated to childhood visual cortex development.
Incorrect - diplopia is double vision, typically due to nerve palsies causing misalignment, not decreased acuity from cortical maldevelopment.

Correct - amblyopia ('lazy eye') is decreased visual acuity due to abnormal development of the visual cortex from abnormal visual experience early in life, such as untreated strabismus; it is the basis for pediatric eye screening.
questions.overview: Amblyopia is decreased visual acuity resulting from abnormal development of the visual cortex due to abnormal visual experience in early childhood, commonly caused by uncorrected strabismus. Early detection through pediatric eye screening and treatment is important to prevent permanent visual impairment.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman with a history of intermittent numbness and weakness presents with double vision. On examination, when asked to look to the right, her left eye fails to adduct past midline, while her right eye demonstrates nystagmus on abduction. Convergence is normal. Which of the following is the most likely site of the lesion?
explanations: Incorrect - a left CN III (oculomotor) palsy would impair adduction with convergence also affected, plus ptosis and pupil involvement, unlike isolated INO where CN III function is otherwise normal.
Incorrect - a left frontal eye field lesion would cause the eyes to deviate toward the side of the lesion (left), not this pattern.
Incorrect - a right abducens nucleus lesion would impair abduction of the right eye and horizontal gaze to the right bilaterally, not isolated adduction failure of the left eye.

Correct - failure of the left eye to adduct on right gaze with nystagmus of the abducting (right) eye is internuclear ophthalmoplegia; the side that cannot adduct localizes the lesion, so this is a left MLF lesion. Convergence is spared because it uses a different pathway that does not involve the MLF. This is a classic presentation of multiple sclerosis, since the MLF is highly myelinated.
Incorrect - a right PPRF lesion would cause an ipsilateral gaze palsy (inability to look right with both eyes), not isolated adduction failure of one eye.
questions.overview: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia results from a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus, causing weak adduction of the ipsilateral eye on contralateral gaze with nystagmus of the abducting eye, while convergence remains intact. It is commonly seen in multiple sclerosis due to the high myelin content of the MLF, and the affected side is identified as the side that cannot adduct.

questions.stem: A young boy with sensorineural hearing loss and hematuria is found to have an eye abnormality related to defective type IV collagen. Which structure of the eye is most likely affected?
explanations: Incorrect - the cornea is not the classic site of type IV collagen abnormality in this syndrome; the lens capsule is specifically affected.
Correct - the lens is surrounded by a capsule composed of type IV collagen, which is abnormal in Alport syndrome, leading to lens problems as part of this hereditary nephritis syndrome.
Incorrect - the retina is not the primary site of type IV collagen abnormality described in Alport syndrome.
Incorrect - the sclera is composed of different collagen and is not the classic site of abnormality in Alport syndrome.
questions.overview: The lens capsule is composed of type IV collagen, and abnormalities in this collagen (as in Alport syndrome, which also causes hereditary nephritis and sensorineural hearing loss) can lead to lens problems.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child is brought in because a family photograph shows a white reflection in one pupil instead of the normal red reflex. Genetic testing reveals mutations in both copies of a tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 13. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanations: Incorrect - retinitis pigmentosa is an inherited degenerative disorder causing progressive night and peripheral vision loss with bone-spicule pigmentation, not leukocoria from a tumor.
Incorrect - retinopathy of prematurity is related to oxygen exposure in preterm infants causing abnormal retinal vessel growth, not a genetic tumor with leukocoria from RB1 mutation.

Correct - retinoblastoma is the most common intraocular malignancy in children, arising from immature retinal cells due to mutations in both RB1 tumor suppressor genes on chromosome 13, and classically presents as leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) in children under 3 years old.
Incorrect - uveal melanoma typically presents in adults, arising from the iris, ciliary body, or choroid, and is associated with light eye color, not leukocoria with RB1 mutations in a young child.
questions.overview: Retinoblastoma is the most common intraocular malignancy in children, caused by mutations in both copies of the RB1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 13 (sporadic or familial), and classically presents as leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) on flash photography or exam in children under age 3.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of a severe headache and double vision. Examination reveals that her right eye is positioned down and out, with complete ptosis of the right eyelid and a dilated, poorly reactive right pupil. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?
explanations: Correct - a CN III palsy with pupillary involvement (dilated, poorly reactive pupil), especially with sudden headache, suggests a compressive etiology such as a posterior communicating artery aneurysm; the parasympathetic fibers run superficially on the nerve and are easily compressed by an external mass.
Incorrect - idiopathic intracranial hypertension classically causes CN VI palsy (esotropia), not CN III palsy with pupil involvement.
Incorrect - MLF demyelination causes internuclear ophthalmoplegia, not a full CN III palsy with ptosis and pupillary dilation.

Incorrect - diabetic ischemic CN III palsy classically spares the pupil (superficial parasympathetic fibers preserved) because ischemia primarily damages the inner nerve fibers, unlike this case with pupillary involvement.
Incorrect - giant cell arteritis causes arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (painless vision loss), not an isolated pupil-involving CN III palsy.
questions.overview: Oculomotor (CN III) nerve palsy causes an eye positioned down and out, ptosis, and possible pupillary dilation depending on etiology. Pupil involvement (dilation) suggests compression, classically from a posterior communicating artery aneurysm, since parasympathetic fibers run superficially and are vulnerable to external compression, whereas pupil-sparing CN III palsy suggests ischemic causes such as diabetes, which spares the superficial fibers.
questions.topic: Oculomotor nerve (CN III) palsy from PCOM aneurysm

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of blurred vision and pain in her left eye that worsens with eye movement. She reports difficulty distinguishing colors in that eye. Examination shows decreased visual acuity in the left eye, and shining a light in the left eye produces less pupillary constriction in both eyes compared to shining the light in the right eye. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of her condition?
explanations: Incorrect - diabetic retinopathy causes gradual vision changes from retinal vascular damage, not acute painful monocular vision loss with an afferent pupillary defect.

Incorrect - giant cell arteritis causes arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy with sudden painless vision loss, typically in patients over 50 with jaw claudication and elevated ESR/CRP, not eye pain with movement.
Incorrect - angle-closure glaucoma causes severe eye pain with halos and a fixed mid-dilated pupil, not an afferent pupillary defect.
Incorrect - herpes zoster ophthalmicus presents with a vesicular rash in the CN V1 distribution and keratitis/uveitis, not isolated painful monocular vision loss with an afferent pupillary defect.

Correct - optic neuritis presents with painful monocular vision loss worsened by eye movement, decreased color vision, and a relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil); it is commonly caused by multiple sclerosis, an inflammatory demyelinating disorder of the optic nerve.
questions.overview: Optic neuritis is inflammation and demyelination of the optic nerve causing monocular vision loss (central more than peripheral), eye pain worsened by movement, decreased color vision, and a relative afferent pupillary defect (positive swinging flashlight test). It is classically associated with multiple sclerosis, diagnosed with OCT and MRI showing optic nerve enhancement, and treated with steroids.

questions.stem: A young woman is found to have a unilaterally dilated pupil that reacts poorly to light but constricts normally with accommodation. Which of the following best describes this condition?
explanations: Correct - Adie's tonic pupil is a dilated pupil with a sluggish/absent response to light but a relatively preserved (better) response to accommodation, most often idiopathic and due to impaired parasympathetic innervation, often from ciliary ganglion pathology.
Incorrect - Horner syndrome causes a small (miotic) pupil with ptosis and anhidrosis, not a dilated pupil.

Incorrect - a relative afferent pupillary defect involves decreased constriction to light in the affected eye during the swinging flashlight test, not this light-near dissociation pattern with dilation.
Incorrect - Argyll Robertson pupil is bilateral, small (miotic), and also shows light-near dissociation but with a constricted rather than dilated pupil; it is associated with neurosyphilis.
questions.overview: Adie's tonic pupil is a dilated pupil with sluggish or absent light reaction but relatively preserved accommodation response, usually idiopathic and caused by disorders of the ciliary ganglion (tumor, inflammation, trauma). It contrasts with Argyll Robertson pupil, which is small/miotic with the same light-near dissociation pattern.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old obese woman presents with a several-week history of daily headaches and pulsatile tinnitus. She also reports intermittent double vision. Examination reveals bilateral optic disc swelling with blurred margins. MRI of the brain shows no mass lesion but reveals bilateral transverse venous sinus stenosis. Which of the following additional findings would be most expected on further evaluation?
options: Afferent pupillary defect with retro-orbital pain worsened by eye movement
Elevated opening pressure on lumbar puncture with normal CSF composition
explanations: Incorrect - an afferent pupillary defect with pain worsened by eye movement describes optic neuritis, not the typical findings of idiopathic intracranial hypertension.
Incorrect - bitemporal hemianopsia results from optic chiasm compression (e.g., pituitary tumor), not idiopathic intracranial hypertension.
Incorrect - bone-spicule pigmentation is characteristic of retinitis pigmentosa, unrelated to idiopathic intracranial hypertension.
Incorrect - a cherry-red spot is seen in central retinal artery occlusion, not idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

Correct - idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri) is characterized by elevated intracranial pressure without an identifiable structural cause; lumbar puncture reveals elevated opening pressure with otherwise normal CSF, which is used for both diagnosis and short-term treatment.
questions.overview: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension classically affects overweight women of childbearing age, presenting with headache, pulsatile tinnitus, papilledema, and sometimes CN VI palsy causing diplopia/esotropia; MRI often shows venous sinus stenosis but no mass, and lumbar puncture shows elevated opening pressure with normal CSF. Treatment includes acetazolamide, weight loss, and in refractory cases, shunting or optic nerve sheath fenestration to preserve vision.

questions.stem: Aqueous humor exits the anterior chamber primarily by draining through which structure?
options: Canal of Schlemm via the trabecular meshwork
explanations: Incorrect - the lacrimal duct drains tears, not aqueous humor.
Incorrect - vortex veins drain choroidal blood, not aqueous humor.
Correct - aqueous humor drains from the anterior chamber through the trabecular meshwork into the canal of Schlemm (scleral venous sinus), and impaired drainage here underlies open-angle glaucoma.
Incorrect - the central retinal vein drains blood from the inner retina, unrelated to aqueous humor outflow.
questions.overview: Aqueous humor flows from the posterior chamber through the pupil into the anterior chamber, then drains through the trabecular meshwork into the canal of Schlemm. Increased resistance to this outflow is the mechanism of open-angle glaucoma, while angle closure physically obstructs this pathway.
questions.topic: Aqueous humor outflow (trabecular meshwork/canal of Schlemm)

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with a history of hypertension and carotid artery stenosis presents with sudden, painless loss of vision in his left eye that occurred over several seconds. Fundoscopic examination reveals a pale retina with a well-demarcated red spot at the macula. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism?
options: Detachment of the neurosensory retina from the retinal pigment epithelium
Occlusion of the central retinal vein
Inflammatory demyelination of the optic nerve
Embolic occlusion of the central retinal artery
explanations: Incorrect - retinal detachment presents with floaters, flashes, and a curtain-like visual field defect, not a cherry-red spot.
Incorrect - central retinal vein occlusion causes a 'blood and thunder' fundus with dilated tortuous veins and diffuse hemorrhages, not a cherry-red spot.
Incorrect - optic neuritis causes painful vision loss with an afferent pupillary defect, not a cherry-red spot.
Incorrect - vitreous hemorrhage from proliferative diabetic retinopathy causes floaters and blurred vision, not this fundoscopic finding.

Correct - sudden painless monocular vision loss with a cherry-red spot at the macula surrounded by pale, ischemic retina is classic for central retinal artery occlusion, most commonly caused by embolism from carotid atherosclerosis.
questions.overview: Central retinal artery occlusion causes sudden, painless monocular vision loss with a pale retina and a cherry-red spot at the macula (also seen in Tay-Sachs and Niemann-Pick disease), most commonly due to embolism from carotid atherosclerosis. It is a retinal ischemic emergency requiring urgent evaluation for embolic sources.

questions.stem: A contact lens wearer presents with eye pain, photophobia, and a corneal infiltrate. Which organism is classically associated with keratitis in this population?
explanations: Correct - Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the classic pathogen causing keratitis in contact lens wearers, presenting with pain, photophobia, red eye, foreign body sensation, and blurred vision; it is sight-threatening and requires prompt treatment.
Incorrect - S. pneumoniae is a common cause of conjunctivitis and other infections but is not the classic contact-lens-associated keratitis pathogen.
Incorrect - N. gonorrhoeae classically causes severe neonatal conjunctivitis, not contact-lens-associated keratitis.
Incorrect - S. aureus is a common cause of bacterial conjunctivitis, not the classic organism for contact lens-associated keratitis.
questions.overview: Keratitis is inflammation of the cornea that can be bacterial, viral, or fungal, and is a sight-threatening emergency presenting with pain, photophobia, red eye, and blurred vision. Contact lens wearers are classically at risk for Pseudomonas aeruginosa keratitis, requiring prompt treatment with appropriate antibiotic eye drops.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with high myopia reports a 2-day history of flashes of light and floaters in her right eye, followed by a curtain-like shadow progressing across her peripheral vision. She denies eye pain. Fundoscopic exam reveals a wrinkled, opacified area of retina with an abrupt change in vessel direction. Which of the following is the most likely predisposing factor for this patient's condition?
explanations: Incorrect - anterior uveitis causes painful red eye with pupillary distortion, not a painless curtain defect.

Correct - posterior vitreous detachment (age-related separation of the vitreous from the retina), especially common with high myopia, can cause traction leading to retinal tears and rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, presenting with floaters, flashes, and a curtain-like visual field defect.
Incorrect - diabetic macular edema causes central vision loss from swelling, not a curtain-like peripheral defect.
Incorrect - open-angle glaucoma causes gradual peripheral vision loss without pain, not acute flashes/floaters/curtain defect.
Incorrect - cataracts cause gradual painless vision loss without floaters or curtain defects.
questions.overview: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, the most common type, results from a retinal tear often associated with posterior vitreous detachment and is a risk in high myopia due to a stretched, thinned retina. Classic symptoms are floaters, light flashes, and a painless curtain-like shadow over the visual field, and it is a surgical emergency to prevent permanent vision loss from photoreceptor hypoxia.

questions.stem: On fundoscopic examination, a patient with chronic open-angle glaucoma is noted to have an increased cup-to-disc ratio of 0.7. Which of the following best describes the significance of this finding?
options: It is diagnostic of central retinal artery occlusion
It reflects glaucomatous optic nerve damage from chronic elevated intraocular pressure
It indicates optic disc swelling from increased intracranial pressure
It is a normal finding not associated with any pathology
explanations: Incorrect - central retinal artery occlusion presents with a pale retina and cherry-red spot, not increased disc cupping.

Correct - an increased cup-to-disc ratio (normal ~0.3, glaucoma >0.6) reflects optic disc cupping from glaucomatous optic nerve damage due to chronically elevated intraocular pressure, characteristic of open-angle glaucoma.
Incorrect - optic disc swelling from increased intracranial pressure describes papilledema, which presents with blurred disc margins, not an increased cup-to-disc ratio.
Incorrect - a cup-to-disc ratio greater than 0.6 is an abnormal finding consistent with glaucomatous damage, not a normal variant.
questions.overview: Open-angle glaucoma causes chronic, painless increased intraocular pressure from increased resistance to aqueous outflow through the trabecular meshwork, leading to progressive optic nerve damage seen as an increased cup-to-disc ratio (disc cupping) on fundoscopy (normal ~0.3, glaucomatous >0.6), with peripheral vision loss preceding central loss.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with a 2-week history of unilateral headache, jaw pain while chewing, and scalp tenderness. She now reports sudden, painless loss of vision in her right eye. Laboratory studies show an ESR of 95 mm/hr. Fundoscopic examination reveals a swollen, pale optic disc. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Observation and risk factor modification only
Temporal artery biopsy with immediate initiation of high-dose corticosteroids
explanations: Incorrect - anti-VEGF injections treat neovascularization (e.g., wet macular degeneration, proliferative diabetic retinopathy), not arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy.
Incorrect - observation alone is appropriate for non-arteritic AION (NAION), not AAION, which is a vision- and life-threatening emergency requiring urgent steroids.
Incorrect - cocaine testing is used to diagnose Horner syndrome, not AAION.
Incorrect - acetazolamide and mannitol treat acute angle-closure glaucoma, not AAION.

Correct - this presentation (elderly woman, headache, jaw claudication, elevated ESR, sudden painless vision loss with a swollen pale disc) is classic for giant cell arteritis causing arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (AAION); diagnosis is confirmed with temporal artery biopsy, but high-dose steroids should be started immediately without waiting for biopsy results to prevent further vision loss and stroke.
questions.overview: Giant cell (temporal) arteritis is a vasculitis in women over 50 causing headache, temporal artery tenderness, jaw claudication, and elevated ESR/CRP; its feared complication is arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (AAION), presenting as sudden painless monocular vision loss with a swollen, pale optic disc. Treatment with high-dose steroids should begin immediately, before biopsy confirmation, to prevent irreversible blindness and stroke.

questions.stem: A patient presents with a red eye. Which finding would favor a diagnosis of scleritis over episcleritis?
options: Isolated, localized redness with an otherwise normal-appearing globe
Severe, boring pain that worsens with eye movement
Mild discomfort with tearing and no discharge
explanations: Incorrect - episcleritis is usually self-limited, whereas scleritis is a more serious, potentially blinding condition requiring treatment of the underlying rheumatologic disease.
Incorrect - this describes the milder presentation of episcleritis, not the more severe scleritis.
Correct - scleritis causes severe 'boring' pain that worsens with eye movement and can spread to the face/head, distinguishing it from the typically mild or painless episcleritis.
Incorrect - mild discomfort with tearing and no discharge is characteristic of episcleritis, not scleritis.
questions.overview: Episcleritis is inflammation of the episcleral layer causing mild redness and discomfort with tearing but no discharge, usually idiopathic and self-limited. Scleritis is deeper inflammation of the sclera causing severe boring pain worsened by eye movement, is potentially blinding, and is often associated with systemic rheumatologic disease requiring treatment.

questions.stem: A patient who cannot focus clearly on distant objects is diagnosed with myopia due to an elongated eyeball. Which type of corrective lens is used to treat this condition?
options: Bifocal lens with a distance-only correction
explanations: Incorrect - bifocal lenses are used to correct presbyopia, which involves difficulty focusing on both near and far objects due to age-related lens stiffening.
Incorrect - cylindrical lenses correct astigmatism, which results from uneven corneal curvature causing multiple focal points, not myopia.

Correct - myopia occurs when the focal point falls in front of the retina (due to an elongated eye or excessive corneal curvature); it is corrected with a negative/concave/diverging lens that moves the focal point back onto the retina.
Incorrect - a convex/converging lens is used to correct hyperopia (farsightedness), not myopia.
questions.overview: Myopia (nearsightedness) occurs when the eye is too long or the cornea too curved, placing the focal point in front of the retina; it is corrected with a concave (diverging) lens. This contrasts with hyperopia, where the focal point falls behind the retina and is corrected with a convex (converging) lens.

questions.stem: Which structure of the eye is primarily responsible for producing aqueous humor and altering the shape of the lens during accommodation?
explanations: Correct - the ciliary body, via its ciliary epithelium, produces aqueous humor secreted into the posterior chamber, and its ciliary muscle changes lens shape during accommodation.
Incorrect - the choroid is a vascular layer that supplies blood to the outer retina and is not involved in aqueous humor production.
Incorrect - the iris controls pupil size via the sphincter and dilator pupillae muscles, not aqueous humor production.
Incorrect - the retinal pigment epithelium supports photoreceptors and absorbs light; it does not produce aqueous humor.
questions.overview: The ciliary body, part of the uvea, has two key functions: its epithelium secretes aqueous humor into the posterior chamber (which flows through the pupil to the anterior chamber and drains via the trabecular meshwork/canal of Schlemm), and its smooth muscle changes lens shape for accommodation. Disruption of aqueous humor dynamics underlies glaucoma.

questions.stem: Following blunt trauma to the eye, a patient is found to have blood layering in the space between the cornea and the iris. What is this finding called?
explanations: Incorrect - hypopyon is an inflammatory (white cell) infiltrate in the anterior chamber, typically seen with keratitis or uveitis, not blood.
Incorrect - chorioretinitis is inflammation of the choroid and retina, typically infectious, unrelated to traumatic bleeding in the anterior chamber.
Incorrect - vitreous hemorrhage is bleeding into the vitreous chamber (between lens and retina), not the anterior chamber.
Correct - hyphema is blood in the anterior chamber (between cornea and iris), commonly caused by trauma and can lead to vision problems and permanent vision loss if severe.
questions.overview: Hyphema refers to blood in the anterior chamber, usually resulting from blunt trauma, and can cause vision problems or permanent vision loss. It is distinguished from hypopyon, which is an inflammatory (not hemorrhagic) infiltrate in the same anatomic space, typically due to keratitis or uveitis.

questions.stem: Shining light into one eye causes bilateral pupillary constriction. Which structure coordinates the consensual (opposite eye) response in this reflex?
options: Pretectal nucleus with bilateral projections to the Edinger-Westphal nuclei
explanations: Correct - light signals travel to the pretectal nucleus in the midbrain, which projects bilaterally to the Edinger-Westphal nuclei, producing both direct (same eye) and consensual (opposite eye) pupillary constriction.
Incorrect - frontal eye fields control voluntary conjugate gaze, not the pupillary light reflex.
Incorrect - the lateral geniculate nucleus relays visual information to the cortex for conscious vision, not the pupillary light reflex.
Incorrect - the pupillary light reflex is a subcortical reflex that does not involve the visual cortex.
questions.overview: The pupillary light reflex is a subcortical, bilateral reflex: light input reaches the pretectal nucleus, which projects to both Edinger-Westphal nuclei, producing simultaneous constriction of both pupils regardless of which eye is illuminated. This pathway is tested clinically with the swinging flashlight test to detect a relative afferent pupillary defect.

questions.stem: A patient with tertiary neurosyphilis is found to have bilateral small pupils that do not constrict in response to light but do constrict with accommodation. This finding is known as which of the following?
explanations: Correct - Argyll Robertson pupil is strongly associated with tertiary neurosyphilis, presenting with bilateral small pupils that fail to constrict to light but do constrict with accommodation ('light-near dissociation'), believed to involve the pretectal nucleus.
Incorrect - Marcus Gunn pupil (relative afferent pupillary defect) shows decreased constriction to light in one eye on swinging flashlight testing, not bilateral light-near dissociation.
Incorrect - Horner syndrome causes unilateral miosis with ptosis and anhidrosis, not bilateral light-near dissociation.
Incorrect - Adie's tonic pupil is dilated (mydriatic), not small, and is usually idiopathic rather than associated with neurosyphilis.
questions.overview: Argyll Robertson pupil is a classic finding in tertiary neurosyphilis, characterized by bilateral small pupils that show light-near dissociation (poor constriction to light but normal constriction with accommodation), thought to involve the pretectal nucleus, which is part of the light reflex pathway but not the accommodation pathway.

questions.stem: A patient with a tall stature, long wingspan, and bilateral lens dislocation is noted on exam to have the lenses displaced upward and outward. Which condition is most consistent with this pattern of lens dislocation?
explanations: Incorrect - congenital rubella syndrome causes cataracts as part of a triad with deafness and cardiac malformations, not lens dislocation.

Incorrect - homocystinuria classically causes downward and inward lens dislocation, not upward and outward, and typically presents with additional findings like thrombosis and intellectual disability.
Incorrect - classic galactosemia presents in infancy with liver failure and cataracts, not lens dislocation.

Correct - Marfan syndrome, an autosomal dominant fibrillin defect causing tall stature and long wingspan, is the most common systemic condition associated with ectopia lentis, classically causing upward and outward lens dislocation.
questions.overview: Ectopia lentis (lens dislocation) is most commonly associated with Marfan syndrome, where it classically occurs upward and outward, in contrast to homocystinuria, where lens dislocation is classically downward and inward; both are due to underlying connective tissue/enzyme defects (fibrillin defect in Marfan, cystathionine beta synthase deficiency in homocystinuria).

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman develops sudden severe right eye pain, blurred vision, and halos around lights while watching a movie in a dark theater. She also reports nausea and vomiting. Exam shows a red eye with a fixed, mid-dilated pupil and a firm globe on palpation. Which of the following medications, if given, would most likely worsen her condition?
explanations: Incorrect - pilocarpine (a muscarinic agonist) constricts the pupil and opens the angle, and is used as treatment.
Incorrect - acetazolamide (a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) decreases aqueous production and is a standard treatment.
Incorrect - mannitol is an osmotic diuretic used to acutely lower intraocular pressure, and is part of treatment.
Incorrect - timolol (a beta blocker) decreases aqueous humor production and is used to treat acute angle-closure glaucoma.
Correct - epinephrine causes mydriasis, which would further close the angle and worsen acute angle-closure glaucoma; it is contraindicated in this condition.
questions.overview: Acute angle-closure glaucoma occurs when the peripheral iris obstructs the trabecular meshwork, causing an abrupt severe rise in intraocular pressure with pain, halos, nausea/vomiting, and a fixed mid-dilated pupil; it is an ophthalmologic emergency. Mydriatic agents (sympathomimetics, anticholinergics) worsen angle closure by further narrowing the drainage angle and are contraindicated, while treatment includes acetazolamide, mannitol, timolol, and pilocarpine.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which pilocarpine lowers intraocular pressure in glaucoma?
options: Muscarinic agonism causing contraction of the ciliary muscle, which opens the trabecular meshwork and increases aqueous outflow
Alpha-2 agonism, decreasing aqueous humor production by the ciliary epithelium
Beta-1 receptor blockade, decreasing aqueous humor production
Carbonic anhydrase inhibition, decreasing aqueous humor synthesis
explanations: Correct - pilocarpine is a muscarinic agonist (parasympathomimetic) that contracts the ciliary muscle, causing miosis and opening the trabecular meshwork to increase aqueous humor drainage.
This describes alpha agonists like brimonidine/apraclonidine, not pilocarpine.
This describes the mechanism of beta blockers like timolol, not pilocarpine.
This describes carbonic anhydrase inhibitors like acetazolamide, not pilocarpine.
questions.overview: Pilocarpine and carbachol are muscarinic agonists (parasympathomimetics) used in glaucoma treatment that contract the ciliary muscle, causing miosis and opening the trabecular meshwork to increase aqueous humor outflow. A common side effect is blurry vision and impaired night vision due to sustained pupillary constriction.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man presents for a routine eye exam with no visual complaints. His father had glaucoma, and he has type 2 diabetes. Tonometry shows IOP of 26 mmHg bilaterally, and fundoscopy reveals a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.7. Which of the following best characterizes the typical risk factor profile and disease course for his most likely diagnosis?
options: Increasing age, family history, and diabetes are major risk factors, and vision loss is typically asymptomatic until peripheral fields are affected
Female sex and pregnancy are the major risk factors, with acute headache and halos
Contact lens use is the major risk factor, with rapid painful corneal ulceration
Young age and hyperopia are the major risk factors, with sudden painful vision loss
Recent ocular trauma is the major risk factor, with hyphema and blurred vision
explanations: Correct - open-angle glaucoma's major risk factors are increased age, family history, and diabetes; it is typically asymptomatic until peripheral (then central) vision loss occurs, matching this patient's elevated IOP and increased cup-to-disc ratio.
This describes acute angle-closure glaucoma, not open-angle glaucoma.
This describes risk factors for Pseudomonas keratitis, unrelated to glaucoma.
This describes risk factors more typical of anatomically predisposed angle-closure glaucoma, which presents acutely and painfully, not open-angle disease.
This describes risk factors for hyphema, not open-angle glaucoma.
questions.overview: Open-angle glaucoma is the most common form of glaucoma, caused by increased resistance to aqueous outflow through the trabecular meshwork. Major risk factors include increasing age, family history, and diabetes, and the disease is typically asymptomatic until peripheral, and later central, vision loss occurs, making screening with tonometry and fundoscopic exam for disc cupping essential.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man notices increasing difficulty reading fine print, requiring him to hold reading material farther away. Which of the following best explains the underlying mechanism of this condition?
options: Opacification of the lens due to accumulation of sorbitol
Corneal curvature that fails to match the size of the eye
Age-related stiffening of the lens, impairing its ability to round and focus on near objects
Progressive elongation of the globe, causing the focal point to fall in front of the retina
explanations: This describes diabetic cataract formation via the polyol pathway, not presbyopia.
This describes the general mechanism of refractive errors like myopia/hyperopia/astigmatism, not the age-related lens stiffening of presbyopia.
Correct - presbyopia results from age-related stiffening of the lens, which impairs the lens's ability to round and increase its optical power for near vision (accommodation).
This describes myopia, not presbyopia.
questions.overview: Presbyopia is the age-related stiffening of the lens that impairs accommodation, making it difficult to focus on near objects such as reading material. It is commonly corrected with bifocal or multifocal lenses that provide distinct zones of optical power for near and distance vision.

questions.stem: An elderly immunocompromised man presents with a prodrome of headache and malaise followed by a vesicular rash along the forehead and tip of the nose, with associated conjunctivitis and keratitis. Which of the following best describes this condition?
options: Autoimmune inflammation of the sclera associated with rheumatoid arthritis
Primary infection with herpes simplex virus type 1 of the optic nerve
Reactivation of cytomegalovirus in an HIV patient with a low CD4 count
Reactivation of varicella-zoster virus involving the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve
explanations: Scleritis is associated with rheumatologic disease but does not present with a vesicular rash along a dermatome.
This describes recurrent ocular HSV disease, a distinct entity caused by HSV-1, not varicella-zoster virus.
CMV retinitis occurs in severely immunocompromised HIV patients with low CD4 counts and presents with retinal hemorrhages and necrosis, not a vesicular dermatomal rash.

Correct - herpes zoster ophthalmicus results from reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus involving the ophthalmic (V1) division of the trigeminal nerve, presenting with a prodrome followed by vesicular rash and ocular involvement (conjunctivitis, uveitis, episcleritis, keratitis), typically in older or immunocompromised patients.
questions.overview: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus results from reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus in the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, typically in older or immunocompromised patients. It presents with a prodrome of headache, malaise, and fever, followed by a vesicular rash, and can cause conjunctivitis, uveitis, episcleritis, and keratitis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the composition and primary function of the vitreous humor?
options: A gel-like substance that is approximately 99% water and helps maintain eye shape and support the retina
A water-like fluid produced by the ciliary epithelium that flows through the pupil to the anterior chamber
A protein-rich fluid produced by the retinal pigment epithelium that nourishes the cornea
A collagen-based membrane that separates the choroid from the sclera
explanations: Correct - vitreous humor is a transparent, gel-like substance, approximately 99% water plus collagen and glycosaminoglycans, that maintains eye shape, supports the retina, and provides shock absorption.
This describes aqueous humor, produced by the ciliary body, not vitreous humor.
Vitreous humor is not produced by the RPE, and it does not nourish the cornea.
This does not describe the vitreous humor, which is a fluid-filled gel, not a membrane.
questions.overview: The vitreous humor is a transparent, gel-like substance filling the space between the lens and retina, composed of about 99% water along with collagen and glycosaminoglycans. It maintains the shape of the eye, supports the retina, transmits light, and provides shock absorption; age-related degeneration of the vitreous is a common cause of floaters.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and obstructive sleep apnea wakes up with painless loss of vision in his right eye. Fundoscopy shows a swollen optic disc. ESR and CRP are within normal limits, and his optic disc is noted to be small and crowded. Which of the following best describes the underlying process and key predisposing factor for his condition?
options: Hypoperfusion of the optic nerve head in a patient with vascular risk factors and a small, crowded ("at risk") optic disc
Embolic occlusion of the central retinal artery from a carotid plaque
Elevated intracranial pressure causing impaired axoplasmic flow
Demyelination of the optic nerve associated with multiple sclerosis
Inflammatory arteritis of the posterior ciliary arteries requiring emergent steroid therapy
explanations: Correct - NAION results from hypoperfusion of the optic nerve head, associated with vascular risk factors (diabetes, hypertension, sleep apnea) and a small "disc at risk"; it typically presents with sudden painless vision loss on awakening and normal inflammatory markers.
CRAO produces a cherry-red spot with a pale retina and is typically embolic, but this patient's swollen disc is consistent with anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, not CRAO.
This describes the mechanism of papilledema, which is bilateral and due to elevated ICP, not this patient's unilateral presentation with vascular risk factors.
MS-related optic neuritis is a demyelinating, painful process typically in younger patients, not matching this vascular risk profile.
This describes AAION from giant cell arteritis, which would show elevated ESR/CRP, not the normal values seen in this patient.
questions.overview: Non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) is caused by hypoperfusion of the optic nerve head and is associated with vascular risk factors such as diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and obstructive sleep apnea, plus a small, crowded "disc at risk." Unlike arteritic AION from giant cell arteritis, ESR/CRP are normal, and it presents as sudden painless monocular vision loss, typically noticed upon awakening, with no specific treatment beyond risk factor management.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with pain that worsens with eye movement and progressive loss of vision in one eye over several days, along with decreased color perception. Exam reveals an afferent pupillary defect. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanations: Acute angle-closure glaucoma presents with severe pain, red eye, halos, and a fixed mid-dilated pupil, not the pattern of vision loss and pain with eye movement described here.
Cataracts are painless and cause gradual vision loss, not the acute painful presentation described.

Correct - optic neuritis presents with monocular vision loss (central more than peripheral), loss of color vision, pain that worsens with eye movement, and an afferent pupillary defect, commonly associated with multiple sclerosis.
Retinal detachment presents with floaters, flashes, and a curtain-like visual field loss, not eye pain with movement or color desaturation.
questions.overview: Optic neuritis is inflammation and demyelination of the optic nerve, commonly associated with multiple sclerosis, presenting with monocular vision loss (central greater than peripheral), loss of color vision, flickering lights, and eye pain that worsens with movement, with an afferent pupillary defect on exam. Diagnosis involves OCT showing decreased retinal layer thickness and MRI showing optic nerve enhancement; treatment is with steroids.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with several weeks of unilateral throbbing headache, scalp tenderness when brushing her hair, and jaw pain while chewing that improves with rest. She also reports a 5-kg weight loss and low-grade fevers. Labs show ESR 95 mm/hr and markedly elevated CRP. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?
options: MRI of the brain with contrast
Lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement
explanations: Fluorescein angiography is not the confirmatory test for GCA described in the notes.
MRI of the brain does not confirm arteritis and is not the diagnostic test for GCA.
Correct - temporal artery biopsy is the diagnostic gold standard for giant cell (temporal) arteritis.
Genetic testing is used for Leber hereditary optic neuropathy, a mitochondrial disorder, not GCA.
LP with opening pressure is used to evaluate idiopathic intracranial hypertension, not GCA.
questions.overview: Giant cell (temporal) arteritis is a vasculitis affecting women over 50, presenting with unilateral headache, temporal artery tenderness, jaw claudication, and elevated ESR/CRP. It can cause arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (AAION), an emergency causing sudden painless monocular vision loss with a swollen, pale disc; diagnosis is confirmed by temporal artery biopsy, and urgent steroids are needed to prevent blindness and stroke.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man develops sudden loss of vision in the left half of his visual field in both eyes after an ischemic stroke. Central (macular) vision is preserved. Which of the following vascular territories and lesion locations best explains this presentation?
options: Bilateral optic nerve demyelination from multiple sclerosis
Right posterior cerebral artery infarct affecting the right optic tract/occipital cortex, with macular sparing due to dual blood supply
Left middle cerebral artery infarct affecting the left optic chiasm
Left posterior communicating artery aneurysm compressing the left oculomotor nerve
Right anterior cerebral artery infarct affecting the right optic nerve
explanations: MS causes optic neuritis, typically monocular vision loss, not bilateral homonymous hemianopsia with macular sparing.

Correct - loss of the left visual field in both eyes indicates a right-sided post-chiasmal lesion (optic tract to occipital cortex); PCA strokes classically spare the macula due to its dual MCA/PCA blood supply.
The optic chiasm is not in MCA territory, and a chiasmal lesion causes bitemporal, not homonymous, field loss.
A PCOM aneurysm compresses CN III, causing ptosis, a dilated pupil, and the eye positioned down and out, not a visual field defect.
The optic nerve is pre-chiasmal; a lesion here causes monocular vision loss, not homonymous hemianopsia, and is not typically due to an ACA infarct.
questions.overview: Homonymous hemianopsia results from lesions posterior to the optic chiasm (optic tract, optic radiations, or occipital cortex) and causes loss of the same-sided visual field in both eyes. PCA strokes affecting the occipital cortex classically spare the macula because of its dual blood supply from the MCA and PCA.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman presents to the ED with acute onset severe right eye pain, headache, nausea, and vomiting after sitting in a dark movie theater. Exam shows a red right eye, hazy cornea, a fixed and mid-dilated pupil, and IOP of 52 mmHg. Which of the following best describes the pathophysiologic mechanism causing her symptoms?
options: Optic nerve demyelination from autoimmune inflammation
Occlusion of the central retinal artery by an embolus
Increased episcleral venous pressure from a carotid-cavernous fistula
Chronic scarring of the trabecular meshwork due to long-standing uveitis
Anteriorly displaced lens causing pupillary block and obstruction of aqueous outflow through the angle
explanations: This describes optic neuritis, which is unrelated to acute angle closure.
CRAO causes sudden painless vision loss with a pale retina and cherry-red spot, not a painful red eye with markedly elevated IOP.
This mechanism is not discussed in the notes as a cause of acute angle-closure glaucoma.
This describes a chronic secondary open-angle process, not the acute pupillary block mechanism of this presentation.

Correct - this is the mechanism of pupillary block in angle-closure glaucoma: the anteriorly displaced lens blocks flow through the pupil, pressure builds in the posterior chamber, and the peripheral iris pushes against the cornea, obstructing the drainage angle.
questions.overview: Acute angle-closure glaucoma occurs when the peripheral iris blocks the trabecular meshwork, often precipitated by pupillary dilation (e.g., dark environments, mydriatic drugs), causing an abrupt increase in IOP. It presents with severe eye pain, halos around lights, a fixed mid-dilated pupil, and nausea/vomiting, and is an ophthalmologic emergency.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man presents with painless, subacute vision loss in one eye that progresses to involve the other eye over the following weeks. His mother has a history of unexplained vision loss at a young age, but his father is unaffected. Which of the following best describes the inheritance pattern of the most likely diagnosis?
explanations: LHON is not autosomal recessive; it follows mitochondrial inheritance.

Correct - Leber hereditary optic neuropathy is caused by mutations in electron transport chain complexes and follows mitochondrial, maternal inheritance, consistent with the mother's history of vision loss and the father being unaffected.
LHON is not autosomal dominant; it follows mitochondrial inheritance.
LHON is not X-linked; it is inherited through mitochondrial (maternal) DNA.
questions.overview: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy is a mitochondrially (maternally) inherited disorder caused by mutations in electron transport chain complexes, typically presenting with painless, subacute monocular vision loss with central scotoma and color vision deficiency between ages 10-30, with the other eye affected within weeks to months. Diagnosis is by genetic testing, and there is no cure.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman is found to have a unilaterally dilated pupil. It reacts poorly to direct light but constricts more briskly when she focuses on a near object. Which of the following best characterizes this pupillary abnormality?
options: Sluggish or absent reaction to light with a relatively preserved, better response to accommodation
Bilateral small pupils with no reaction to light but normal reaction to accommodation
Fixed and mid-dilated pupil with severe eye pain
Normal reaction to light with absent reaction to accommodation
explanations: Correct - Adie's tonic pupil is a dilated pupil with sluggish/absent light reaction but a relatively better response to accommodation ("light-near dissociation" favoring accommodation), most often idiopathic.
This describes the Argyll Robertson pupil, associated with neurosyphilis, not Adie's tonic pupil (which is typically unilateral and dilated, not bilateral and small).
This describes acute angle-closure glaucoma, a painful condition unrelated to Adie's pupil.
This is the reverse of the actual finding in Adie's pupil, which has an abnormal, not normal, light reaction.
questions.overview: Adie's tonic pupil is a dilated pupil caused by impaired parasympathetic innervation, most commonly idiopathic, though it can result from disorders of the ciliary ganglion (tumor, inflammation, trauma, surgery, infection). It characteristically shows a poor/sluggish reaction to light but a relatively preserved reaction to accommodation, distinguishing it from other causes of anisocoria.

questions.stem: A patient with wet (neovascular) age-related macular degeneration is being started on treatment to reduce abnormal blood vessel growth. Which of the following classes of medication is most appropriate?
options: Oral antioxidant vitamin supplements (vitamin C/E, zinc, copper)
Anti-VEGF agents such as ranibizumab or bevacizumab
explanations: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors are used for glaucoma, not AMD.
Antioxidant vitamin/mineral supplementation may help slow dry AMD progression, not wet AMD, which requires anti-VEGF therapy.
Topical beta blockers are used for glaucoma, not AMD.
Correct - wet AMD is treated with anti-VEGF agents (ranibizumab, bevacizumab) and laser therapy, targeting the increased VEGF-driven retinal neovascularization that characterizes this form of AMD.
questions.overview: Wet (neovascular) AMD, though less common than dry AMD, can progress rapidly due to a break in Bruch's membrane and VEGF-driven retinal neovascularization, causing metamorphopsia and vision loss from vessel leakage/hemorrhage. It is treated with laser therapy and anti-VEGF agents such as ranibizumab and bevacizumab, in contrast to dry AMD, which has no specific treatment beyond antioxidant supplementation.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis presents with a localized area of redness in one eye, mild tearing, and mild discomfort, with no discharge and no significant pain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanations: Bacterial conjunctivitis typically presents with purulent discharge, which this patient does not have.
Scleritis presents with severe, "boring" pain that worsens with eye movement and can be sight-threatening, unlike this patient's mild symptoms.
Correct - episcleritis presents with localized redness, tearing, and mild or no pain/discomfort, often idiopathic but associated with rheumatoid arthritis, and is usually self-limited.
Keratitis presents with significant pain, photophobia, and foreign body sensation, often in contact lens wearers, not matching this presentation.
questions.overview: Episcleritis is acute inflammation of the episcleral layer between the conjunctiva and sclera, causing localized redness and tearing with mild or no pain; it is usually idiopathic and self-limited but can be associated with rheumatoid arthritis. It is distinguished from the more severe, painful scleritis by its milder course and lack of vision-threatening potential.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old obese woman presents with several weeks of progressive headache and pulsatile tinnitus, plus intermittent horizontal diplopia. Fundoscopy reveals bilateral optic disc swelling with blurred margins. MRI of the brain shows no mass lesion but does reveal bilateral transverse venous sinus narrowing. Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?
options: Lumbar puncture to measure opening pressure
Genetic testing for mitochondrial DNA mutations
explanations: Correct - after neuroimaging rules out a mass lesion or other structural cause, lumbar puncture is used to confirm elevated intracranial pressure and can also provide short-term symptomatic relief in idiopathic intracranial hypertension.
Genetic testing is used for Leber hereditary optic neuropathy, not IIH.
Fluorescein angiography is not the diagnostic test described for IIH in the notes.
Tonometry measures intraocular pressure, which is not the mechanism of visual loss in IIH (that involves intracranial, not intraocular, pressure).
Temporal artery biopsy is used to diagnose giant cell arteritis, not IIH.
questions.overview: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri) presents classically in obese women of childbearing age with headache, pulsatile tinnitus, diplopia (often CN VI palsy), and papilledema from impaired axoplasmic flow at the optic nerve head, without a mass lesion on imaging (though venous sinus stenosis is often seen). Diagnosis requires MRI to exclude other causes of elevated ICP, followed by lumbar puncture to confirm and, if needed, transiently lower the opening pressure; treatment includes acetazolamide, weight loss, and, in refractory cases, shunting or optic nerve sheath fenestration.

questions.stem: A patient with long-standing poorly controlled hypertension undergoes a routine fundoscopic exam. Which of the following findings is classically associated with hypertensive retinopathy?
explanations: "Blood and thunder" fundus is characteristic of central retinal vein occlusion, not hypertensive retinopathy.
Bone-spicule pigmentation is characteristic of retinitis pigmentosa, not hypertensive retinopathy.
Correct - arteriovenous nicking, along with arteriolar narrowing, hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, hard exudates, and microaneurysms, is a classic fundoscopic finding of hypertensive retinopathy.
A cherry-red spot is classic for central retinal artery occlusion (and Tay-Sachs/Niemann-Pick disease), not hypertensive retinopathy.
questions.overview: Hypertensive retinopathy results from sclerosis and fibrinoid necrosis of retinal vessels due to chronic hypertension, with classic fundoscopic findings including arteriovenous nicking, arteriolar narrowing and wall thickening, hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, and hard exudates; severe cases can cause papilledema requiring emergent treatment.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with new floaters and occasional flashes of light in one eye, with no pain or vision loss. This is most consistent with which of the following processes?
options: Posterior vitreous detachment, an age-related separation of the vitreous gel from the retina
explanations: Correct - posterior vitreous detachment is a common, often benign, age-related process in which the vitreous gel separates from the retina, causing floaters and flashes of light; it can occasionally lead to retinal tears or detachment.
Endophthalmitis presents with pain, redness, and hypopyon, not isolated floaters and flashes.
Angle-closure glaucoma presents with severe eye pain, redness, and halos, not painless floaters and flashes.
CRAO causes sudden painless but severe vision loss, not isolated floaters and flashes.
questions.overview: Posterior vitreous detachment occurs when the aging vitreous gel separates from the retina, most often producing floaters and flashes of light and typically remaining asymptomatic and benign. However, traction on the retina during this process can cause retinal tears, so patients should be monitored for progression to retinal detachment.

questions.stem: Following a large right middle cerebral artery stroke affecting the frontal eye field, a patient's eyes are noted to deviate persistently in which direction?
options: Toward the right (side of the lesion)
Toward the left (away from the lesion)
The eyes remain midline and unaffected
explanations: Correct - a destructive lesion of the frontal eye field causes both eyes to deviate toward the side of the lesion, since the contralateral (unaffected) frontal eye field's input is unopposed.
This is the pattern seen with stimulation (e.g., a seizure) of the frontal eye field, not a destructive lesion such as stroke.
The described deviation pattern is not associated with FEF lesions in the notes.
FEF lesions characteristically cause eye deviation, not a neutral midline position.
questions.overview: The frontal eye fields (Brodmann area 8), supplied by the MCA, project to the contralateral PPRF to initiate conjugate gaze to the opposite side. A destructive lesion (e.g., MCA stroke) causes both eyes to deviate toward the side of the lesion, while stimulation (e.g., seizure activity) causes deviation to the opposite side.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a well-established risk factor for the development of cataracts?
explanations: Hyperopia is a refractive error and is not listed as a cataract risk factor in the notes.
Correct - chronic corticosteroid use is a recognized risk factor for cataract formation, along with older age, smoking, alcohol use, excessive sunlight exposure, trauma, and infection.
Older age, not young age, is a risk factor for cataracts.
Low iris melanin (light eye color) is a risk factor for uveal melanoma, not cataracts.
questions.overview: Cataracts are a painless opacification of the lens leading to decreased vision, with risk factors including older age, smoking, alcohol use, excessive sunlight exposure, corticosteroid use, trauma, and infection. Treatment is surgical lens replacement.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has mild ptosis and miosis of the left eye, with decreased sweating on the left side of his face. Apraclonidine eye drops are applied to both eyes. In the affected left eye, the pupil dilates, while the normal right eye shows minimal change. Which of the following best explains this finding?
options: Blockade of muscarinic receptors on the sphincter pupillae
Impaired parasympathetic input to the ciliary ganglion
Direct stimulation of the Edinger-Westphal nucleus
Denervation supersensitivity of alpha-1 receptors on the dilator pupillae due to loss of sympathetic innervation
Increased intraocular pressure causing mechanical pupil dilation
explanations: Muscarinic blockade would affect the sphincter pupillae and is not the mechanism of the apraclonidine test.
Horner syndrome is a sympathetic, not parasympathetic, lesion; the ciliary ganglion is not involved.
The Edinger-Westphal nucleus governs parasympathetic pupillary constriction and is unrelated to this sympathetic test.

Correct - apraclonidine, an alpha-1 agonist, causes exaggerated dilation of the miotic Horner pupil due to denervation supersensitivity of the dilator pupillae, while it has little effect on a normal pupil.
The test is pharmacologic, not related to intraocular pressure.
questions.overview: Horner syndrome results from disruption of the oculosympathetic pathway, producing miosis, ptosis, and anhidrosis. Apraclonidine, an alpha-1 agonist, is used diagnostically: it paradoxically dilates the miotic Horner pupil due to denervation supersensitivity while causing little change in the normal eye, confirming the pupillary dilator muscle itself is functional.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic open-angle glaucoma is prescribed epinephrine eye drops. Which of the following is an important contraindication or risk associated with this medication?
options: It is contraindicated in diabetic patients due to risk of hypoglycemia
It is the first-line treatment for acute angle-closure glaucoma
It commonly causes profound bradycardia when used topically
It should never be given in angle-closure glaucoma because it dilates the pupil and can worsen angle closure
explanations: The notes do not describe a contraindication related to diabetes or hypoglycemia for epinephrine eye drops.
Epinephrine is contraindicated, not first-line, in angle-closure glaucoma because it worsens angle closure by dilating the pupil.
This is not a described complication of topical epinephrine in the notes.
Correct - epinephrine, a mixed alpha-beta agonist, dilates the pupil and should never be given in closed-angle glaucoma because it worsens angle closure.
questions.overview: Epinephrine is a mixed alpha-beta agonist used in open-angle glaucoma that initially raises aqueous humor via a beta effect before later causing ciliary body vasoconstriction and decreased aqueous production. Because it dilates the pupil, it is contraindicated in angle-closure glaucoma, where it would worsen angle closure and precipitate an acute attack.

questions.stem: A contact lens wearer presents with eye pain and a foreign body sensation after removing her lenses. Which of the following is the best method to confirm the diagnosis of corneal abrasion?
options: Fluorescein dye staining examined under blue light
explanations: The swinging flashlight test detects an afferent pupillary defect, not a corneal abrasion.
Tonometry measures intraocular pressure and is used to evaluate for glaucoma, not corneal abrasions.
Correct - corneal abrasions are visualized using fluorescein dye, which stains the area of epithelial defect, examined under blue light.
Temporal artery biopsy is used to diagnose giant cell arteritis, unrelated to corneal abrasion.
questions.overview: Corneal abrasions are common among contact lens wearers and cause significant pain due to the dense sensory innervation of the corneal epithelium. Diagnosis is made using fluorescein dye and blue light examination, and abrasions can become secondarily infected with Pseudomonas, often treated prophylactically with ciprofloxacin eye drops.

questions.stem: An infant with classic galactosemia develops cataracts. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of cataract formation in this condition?
options: Excess glucose directly precipitates as crystals within the lens fibers
Deficient type IV collagen in the lens capsule leads to lens rupture
Galactose is converted to galactitol by aldose reductase, which accumulates in the lens and increases osmolarity
Autoimmune destruction of lens epithelial cells
explanations: Glucose does not directly precipitate as crystals; cataract formation in sugar disorders is due to osmotic accumulation of sugar alcohols, not direct crystal precipitation.
Defective type IV collagen describes Alport syndrome's lens involvement, not galactosemia.

Correct - in galactosemia, galactose is metabolized by aldose reductase to galactitol, which accumulates in the lens, increases osmolarity, and draws in water, leading to cataract formation, analogous to the sorbitol pathway in diabetes.
Cataract formation in galactosemia is a metabolic/osmotic process, not autoimmune.
questions.overview: Classic galactosemia and galactokinase deficiency both cause cataracts through accumulation of galactitol, produced from galactose by aldose reductase in the lens, which raises lens osmolarity and draws in water. Classic galactosemia presents in infancy with liver failure and cataracts, while galactokinase deficiency is milder, with cataracts as the main problem in childhood/young adulthood.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with a history of relapsing neurologic symptoms is asked to look to the right. Her right eye abducts normally but shows nystagmus, while her left eye fails to adduct past the midline. Convergence is intact. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis and lesion location?
options: Left PPRF lesion with complete gaze palsy
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia due to a lesion of the left medial longitudinal fasciculus
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia due to a lesion of the right medial longitudinal fasciculus
explanations: A PPRF lesion causes complete gaze palsy to that side (loss of both adduction and abduction), not an isolated adduction deficit with preserved convergence.

Correct - the eye that cannot adduct (left) has the MLF lesion; convergence is spared because it uses a different pathway, and the abducting eye shows nystagmus, classic for INO, commonly caused by MS.
The affected (non-adducting) eye is the left eye, so the lesion is on the left, not the right.
A frontal eye field lesion causes both eyes to deviate toward the lesion side, not an isolated adduction deficit.
A CN VI palsy would impair abduction of the affected eye, not adduction of the opposite eye, and would not spare convergence via the MLF pathway logic.
questions.overview: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia results from a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus, which connects the CN VI nucleus to the contralateral CN III nucleus for conjugate horizontal gaze. It produces impaired adduction of the eye ipsilateral to the lesion with nystagmus of the contralateral abducting eye, while convergence remains intact; it is commonly seen in multiple sclerosis due to the MLF's high degree of myelination.

questions.stem: Timolol is used in the treatment of glaucoma. Which of the following best describes its mechanism of action?
options: Contracts the ciliary muscle to open the trabecular meshwork
Increases aqueous humor outflow via the uveoscleral pathway
Decreases aqueous humor production by blocking beta receptors on the ciliary epithelium
Reduces cell stiffness in the trabecular meshwork to increase outflow
explanations: This describes the mechanism of muscarinic agonists like pilocarpine, not timolol.
This describes the mechanism of prostaglandin analogues (e.g., latanoprost), not timolol.

Correct - timolol is a beta blocker that decreases aqueous humor production by blocking beta receptors on the ciliary epithelium (sympathetic stimulation normally increases aqueous production via beta receptors).
This describes the mechanism of rho kinase inhibitors, not timolol.
questions.overview: Beta blockers such as timolol, betaxolol, and carteolol lower intraocular pressure by blocking beta receptors on the ciliary epithelium, decreasing aqueous humor production (sympathetic beta-2 stimulation normally increases fluid production, particularly relevant during fight-or-flight responses).

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man reports progressive difficulty seeing at night and a gradually constricting visual field since childhood. Fundoscopy reveals dark, bone-spicule-shaped pigment deposits in the peripheral retina, disc pallor, and attenuated retinal vessels. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanations: Retinoblastoma is a childhood intraocular malignancy presenting with leukocoria, not progressive night blindness and bone-spicule pigmentation.
CRVO causes sudden painless vision loss with a "blood and thunder" fundus, not progressive night blindness since childhood.
AMD affects central vision (macula) in older patients and does not present with bone-spicule pigmentation or childhood onset.

Correct - retinitis pigmentosa is an inherited degenerative retinal disorder causing progressive loss of night and peripheral vision beginning in childhood, with bone-spicule pigmentation, disc pallor, and retinal vessel attenuation on fundoscopy.
questions.overview: Retinitis pigmentosa is an inherited degenerative retinal disorder caused by apoptosis of photoreceptors, leading to progressive night and peripheral vision loss (constricted visual field) beginning in childhood, with most patients legally blind by age 40.
