Fundoscopy classically shows bone-spicule pigmentation, optic disc pallor, and retinal vessel attenuation, and there is no cure.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with high myopia reports a sudden shower of floaters and flashes of light in his left eye over the past day, now followed by a curtain-like shadow spreading across his peripheral vision. Fundoscopy shows a wrinkled, opacified area of retina with altered vessel direction. Which of the following best explains the mechanism underlying his vision loss?
options: Separation of the neurosensory retina from the retinal pigment epithelium, leading to loss of choroidal blood supply and photoreceptor hypoxia
Autoimmune demyelination of the optic nerve
Occlusion of the central retinal artery by an embolus from the carotid artery
Increased intraocular pressure causing optic nerve cupping
Accumulation of drusen between Bruch's membrane and the retinal pigment epithelium
explanations: Correct - retinal detachment involves separation of the neurosensory retina from the RPE, cutting off the choroidal blood supply and causing photoreceptor hypoxia and degeneration.
This describes optic neuritis, unrelated to this presentation.
This describes CRAO, which causes acute painless vision loss with a cherry-red spot, not floaters, a curtain, and retinal wrinkling.
This describes the mechanism of glaucoma, not retinal detachment.
This describes dry AMD pathophysiology, not retinal detachment.
questions.overview: Retinal detachment separates the neurosensory retina from the underlying RPE, disrupting the choroidal blood supply and causing photoreceptor hypoxia and degeneration. Rhegmatogenous detachment, the most common type, follows a retinal tear often associated with posterior vitreous detachment and high myopia, presenting with floaters, flashes, and curtain-like visual field loss requiring urgent surgical repair.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with hypertension presents with sudden painless loss of vision in one eye. Fundoscopic exam reveals diffuse retinal hemorrhages in all four quadrants, dilated and tortuous retinal veins, and optic disc edema. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanations: Retinal detachment shows an opacified, wrinkled retina with floaters and curtain-like vision loss, not diffuse hemorrhage in all quadrants.
BRVO causes a sectoral, wedge-shaped hemorrhage limited to the distribution of one vessel, not diffuse involvement of all four quadrants.
Correct - the "blood and thunder" fundus with hemorrhages in all quadrants, dilated tortuous veins, and disc edema describes central retinal vein occlusion.
CRAO produces a cherry-red spot with a pale retina from arterial ischemia, not diffuse hemorrhages in all quadrants.
Diabetic retinopathy shows microaneurysms, dot-blot hemorrhages, and cotton-wool spots, not the diffuse "blood and thunder" pattern described.
questions.overview: CRVO usually results from a primary thrombotic occlusion of the central retinal vein, producing the classic "blood and thunder" fundus - engorged, tortuous veins with hemorrhages in all quadrants and possible disc edema. It presents with sudden, painless vision loss and is distinguished from BRVO, which is localized to a single vascular sector.

questions.stem: A patient is unable to move her left eye laterally on exam, and the left eye appears pulled medially at rest. Which cranial nerve palsy best explains this finding?
explanations: Correct - the abducens nerve innervates the lateral rectus muscle; its palsy impairs lateral eye movement (abduction), and the affected eye may be pulled medially at rest due to unopposed medial rectus action.
CN IV palsy affects the superior oblique, causing difficulty looking down and in, with compensatory head tilt, not an inability to abduct the eye.
CN III palsy causes the eye to rest down and out with ptosis and a dilated pupil, not a medially deviated eye unable to abduct.
The optic nerve carries visual signals and does not control eye movement; a lesion here causes vision loss, not diplopia from muscle weakness.
questions.overview: The abducens nerve (CN VI) innervates the lateral rectus muscle, responsible for eye abduction. Palsy of this nerve causes an inability to move the affected eye laterally, with the eye often pulled medially at rest, and symptoms of diplopia that worsen on horizontal gaze.

questions.stem: A child with a marfanoid body habitus, developmental delay, and markedly elevated plasma homocysteine is found to have bilateral lens dislocation. Which direction of lens dislocation is classically associated with this condition?
options: Directly anterior into the anterior chamber
explanations: Anterior dislocation into the anterior chamber is not the classic direction described for homocystinuria.
Upward and outward lens dislocation is classic for Marfan syndrome, not homocystinuria.
Correct - homocystinuria, caused by cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency, classically causes downward and inward lens dislocation.
Posterior dislocation into the vitreous is not the classic direction described for homocystinuria.
questions.overview: Homocystinuria results from cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency, causing markedly elevated homocysteine levels and a marfanoid body habitus. Unlike Marfan syndrome's upward/outward lens dislocation, homocystinuria classically causes downward and inward ectopia lentis.
